newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberia factions focus on disarmament, elections.
newsitem.headline: Liberia factions focus on disarmament, elections.

text.p: Liberian faction leader Alhaji Kromah handed over heavy weapons to West African peacekeepers and told his supporters that he was ready to stand in elections planned by May.

The handover ceremony in Kromah's northwestern stronghold on the border with Guinea on Saturday was the latest in a series of moves agreed by Liberia's faction leaders under pressure from West African leaders to end more than six years of civil war.
Both Kromah and Charles Taylor, the man who launched the war in 1989, have said they plan to run for president.
"I am seriously available and I think I'm qualified to represent you and will do so when the appropriate time comes," Kromah told supporters who urged him to stand.
But first the different factions must disarm. The latest deal signed in Nigeria's capital Abuja on August 17 gives them until January to do so.
"We have decided to first disarm the most important battalion in our organisation," Kromah told Saturday's handover ceremony. "The exercise will continue until we have totally disarmed."
Kromah said that if the Nigerian-led peacekeepers were now deployed in the west, "by October 1 you would not have seen a pistol in our territory".

West African leaders, frustrated by the collapse of a dozen peace deals, rallied Liberia's warlords round a revamped deal and threatened individual sanctions against any faction leader who derails the peace process.
They agreed to raise the size of the peacekeeping force from 10,000 to 18,000 men but so far lack of numbers mean that the bulk of the force's men are deployed in or around the capital Monrovia.
General Samuel Victor Malu, commander of the ECOMOG peacekeeping force, said in Voinjama on Saturday the disarmament should continue even if his men had not yet deployed.
"The process of disarmament as you have done today should continue and not wait for our deployment," he said, adding: "You don't have to wait for other factions."
Heavy mortars, anti-aircraft guns and rocket-propelled grenades were among arms handed over. Ruth Perry, newly installed head of the State Council, attended the ceremony.
The war has killed well over 150,000 people in Liberia, which was founded by freed American slaves in 1847. Over half the pre-war population of 2.5 million have been driven from their homes.
Taylor and Kromah are vice-chairman on the transitional ruling State Council and their fighters were at the heart of clashes that killed hundreds of people in the capital Monrovia in April and May.

Their opponents were an alliance from the Krahn ethnic group, which broke the stranglehold on power of the freed slaves descendents and ruled Liberia during the 1980s. The fighting unleashed an orgy of looting on the capital.

In another sign of peace, Kromah's Mandingo wing of ULIMO, which formed in 1991 as an anti-Taylor alliance, signed a peace deal with Roosevelt Johnson's ULIMO-J Krahn wing on Friday. "We have agreed to come back as one," Kromah said at that ceremony.

There are an estimated 60,000 armed fighters in Liberia, with Taylor commanding the largest force. Taylor, who has been travelling abroad, has promised to start disarming his men in two weeks time when he expects to demobilise about 3,000.
